record.file_problem: none; the full post and comments are present. Some referenced plots and appendices are not included in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports results on feature absorption and on how SAE features correspond across SAE sizes, which refine and qualify the claim that dictionary features are complete, stable units. It also tests recovery of SAE features in a language model, but does not test superposition geometry itself.
record.gate_note: The reported qualitative outcomes and the .98 correlation are extractable. The toy decoder-cosine plots and the language-model mean-max-correlation and FVU graphs have no numeric values in the supplied text; only the text-described outcomes are recorded. Reconstruction-quality results are not rows because they do not measure a claim version.
record.test_reason: In vanilla SAEs, both in a toy model with known features and in a TinyStories LM, the post shows latents developing absorption holes and fragmenting as width grows. This bears on V5: SAE latents are not stable, canonical units across dictionary sizes. The Matryoshka results measure the author's own method against vanilla SAEs, not the claim. The toy features are orthogonal with no superposition, so V1, V2 and V4 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The author concludes that vanilla SAEs suffer absorption and fragmentation as width grows. Matryoshka SAEs avoid absorption in the toy model; the abstract says 'completely', later qualified to most runs. On TinyStories they reduce absorption and better preserve abstract features, with slightly worse FVU at fixed L0. The author calls for validation on larger models and more data.
record.recipe_differences: Uses sparse autoencoders trained on random prefixes of latents with summed losses, rather than testing the original toy-model superposition setup. The post uses log sparsity loss for both its vanilla and Matryoshka SAEs. It includes a toy absorption setup and a TinyStories application.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by SAE type and language-model location; the Matryoshka advantage is reported for most, not all, locations. Toy-model matching is reported on most runs, not all.

fits_no_version.finding: Matryoshka (nested-prefix) SAE training reduces absorption and better preserves small-SAE features than vanilla SAEs. It does so on most toy runs and at most LM locations, at the cost of worse FVU at fixed L0.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Which latents an SAE learns depends on its training objective; hierarchical prefix losses reduce absorption.

record.peer_reviewed: Alignment Forum; peer-review status not stated
record.problems: The author says the SAEs were trained on 100M tokens, one-third of TinyStories, and calls for validation on larger, more realistic language models with more data. The language model is a 4-layer TinyStories model. Several quantitative comparisons are available only in plots or linked appendices not present in the supplied text. Toy-model success is not universal, and the post notes unresolved absorption and feature-ordering issues.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows omitted. Numerical values from the referenced mean-max-correlation, decoder-cosine, and FVU plots are not present in the supplied text.

untested.parts: No superposition geometry. Toy features are orthogonal, with no sparsity-dependent transition.
No test of capacity competition or polysemantic neurons.
No test of non-capacity causes of polysemanticity.
Assumes SAEs recover model features. Does not test that features are distributed across neurons or that sparse features exist.
Does not test stability across seeds or training runs, or completeness of a dictionary beyond width comparisons.
No comparison of 1-D and multi-dimensional features.

missing.what: Author states absorption/fragmentation is a 'consistent pattern of failure' across many latents (tree_view examples), not only the female-names case.

record.verdict_notes: The toy model has no superposition, so it is relevant only to V5, as a dictionary-recovery test with known ground truth. In a comment, Chanin reports that narrow SAEs also merge child directions into parent latents. The author confirms residual mixing even with all prefixes. This further limits Matryoshka, but it comes from comments, not the post's main results. Bussmann's comment reports Gemma-2-2B absorption improvements but gives no numbers.

versions.untested_parts: No test of overcomplete sparse features being stored as overlapping, nearly orthogonal directions, or of a sparsity-dependent geometric transition.
Does not test polysemantic neurons as a consequence of capacity competition, or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Does not test other causes of polysemantic neurons.
Tests SAE recovery of features in a TinyStories language model, but not whether model features are spread across many neurons; no broader set of real models is tested.

Tests whether SAE features correspond across widths and whether they have absorption holes or fragment. Does not establish that any SAE feature set is complete, stable across training runs, or a canonical representation.
Does not compare one-dimensional features with multidimensional features.

relationships.reason: Parent latents fail to fire when children fire (absorption holes), so the vanilla SAE does not recover the true features (r1).
relationships.display_finding: Parent latents failed to fire when their children fired, leaving absorption holes, so the vanilla SAE did not recover the true features.

relationships.condition: Vanilla SAEs of increasing width, TinyStories 4-layer model
relationships.reason: The abstract female-words latent develops holes at 1000 latents and is replaced by a 'she'-only latent at 25k (r3, r5). Latents are width-dependent, not canonical.
relationships.display_finding: An abstract female-words latent developed holes at 1,000 latents and was replaced by a 'she'-only latent at 25k, so latents depended on width rather than being canonical.
